title: Equalising self and other
hook: all want happiness and not pain, just as I do (Bodhicaryavatara 8)
tomorrow: is a stranger's pain any of my business?

segments.voice: Yesterday: why cling. People meet and part like travelers at an inn; love them with an open hand. Now a closer look at the travelers.
screen: `TRAVELERS AT AN INN.` → `A CLOSER LOOK AT THEM.`

segments.voice: Scroll any comment section and people look impossibly different: other cities, other opinions, each one sure the others are wrong. Some of them you'd cross the street to avoid. Shantideva's meditation chapter makes an odd move here. He has spent pages on the forest and solitude. Then, right where you'd expect him to go deeper inward, he turns to everyone else, and says they aren't different from you in the one way that matters most. Which way?
screen: `A COMMENT SECTION.` → `EVERYONE LOOKS DIFFERENT.` → `AN ODD TURN OUTWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in plain words: first, practice seeing self and other as equal. All of us want happiness. None of us wants pain. Just as I do. That's the puzzle solved. For a bodhisattva, the road to a settled mind runs straight through other people, because what keeps the mind restless is a quiet belief: my happiness is the one that counts. Shantideva questions his own mind. When happiness is dear to me and to others alike, what's so special about me that I chase it only for myself? When fear and pain are unwanted by me and by others alike, why protect only me? He isn't saying your wants don't matter. He's saying they matter for the same reason everyone's do. The barista. The driver who cut you off. The cousin you argue with. Different faces, the same two wishes underneath. In Sanskrit the practice is called paratmasamata, the sameness of other and self. It's a meditation, not a mood, so it's practiced on purpose, one person at a time.
screen: `FIRST: SEE SELF AND OTHER AS EQUAL.` · `ALL WANT HAPPINESS, NOT PAIN.` · `WHAT'S SO SPECIAL ABOUT ME?` · `ONE PERSON AT A TIME.` · then, large: `JUST AS I DO.`

segments.voice: Bring one ordinary person from this week to mind: the one who served your coffee, or sat across from you on the bus. Quietly, out loud if you can, say: this person wants to be happy, just as I do. This person doesn't want to suffer, just as I do. Keep their face in mind as you breathe.
Equalizing self and other: Shantideva's meditation on seeing that everyone wants happiness and not pain, the same as you.
Hold on to this: just as I do, different faces with the same two wishes. Thirty-eight days into the guide.

screen: `DAY 1493 COUNTS.` → `SHANTIDEVA'S GUIDE · 38 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: IS A STRANGER'S PAIN ANY OF MY BUSINESS?`

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhist teaching, equalizing self and other is practiced as a reflection, often recalling a friend, a stranger and a difficult person in turn and seeing the same wish for happiness in each.

match.prompt: the same two wishes — tap the pairs.

myth: Shantideva says your own happiness doesn't matter
your wants matter for the same reason everyone's do.
he asks what's so special about me that I chase happiness only for myself
happiness is dear to me and to others alike.

fork.setup: a coworker snaps at you during a hard week. using 'just as I do', what's the first move?
options: notice she wants this week to go well too, and soften before you reply.
stay quiet and wait for her to apologize first, to keep things equal.
decide her feelings are her business, not yours, and move on.
fork.reveal: equalizing starts by seeing the same two wishes in her: to be happy, not to suffer. that's the ground the kind reply grows from.

original.note: Sanskrit: the sameness of other and self.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone is equal, a nice slogan.
what it means: a meditation of seeing, in each person, the same wish for happiness and freedom from pain.
what a scholar hears: in the guide, equalizing comes first and prepares the more radical exchange of self and other a few verses on.
guess: seeing that others want happiness just as you do
giving away all you own so that everyone is equal
treating everyone the same, with no favorites

chat.says: new kid in art keeps asking to borrow my good markers. it's so annoying. he's always hovering.
options: he wants his piece to turn out well, just as you do. lend one, maybe show him a trick.
treat him exactly like yourself: give him all your markers, every time he asks.
ignore it. equal means you don't owe him more than you owe anyone else.
chat.meaning: Equalizing self and other starts with seeing he wants things to go well, just as Mai does. That's the ground for kindness.
